correctness.rationale: For every vertex on B, all neighbors are exactly A, so each color count on A must be ≤floor(m/2); symmetrically B color capacity is floor(n/2). If total k color capacity on either shore < shore size, full coloring impossible. If capacity≥size, any partial nonfull shore uses fewer than size units and cannot have every color saturated, leaving a universally legal color at every uncolored shore vertex. Therefore neither adversarial choices nor interleaving create dead ends; formula and parity threshold follow for all m,n≥2. Boundary m=n=2 gives 2; any odd shore requires 3. Independently enumerated reachable count states for s=2..11, k=1..5.
residual_risks: The proof relies on the exact strong neighborhood-majority definition; results do not hold automatically on general bipartite graphs.

value.rationale: Complete bipartite graphs form a canonical two-parameter test of a new adversarial coloring game. A sharp parity transition and the stronger theorem that every legal partial play is extendible give a complete game dynamics classification, not merely a static palette count. Though short capacity proof is simple, it resolves a mathematically motivated, nontrivial distinction between static feasibility and adversarial completion.

final_claim: In strong-majority vertex coloring game for K_(m,n), m,n>=2, every legal play can be completed iff k*floor(m/2)>=m and k*floor(n/2)>=n; minimal game palette size is 2 for both sides even and 3 otherwise.
limitations: For m,n>=2 only; stars have degree-one issues.
More general bipartite games may have genuine strategic traps.
